platforms.title: Why Does Melasma Get Darker Even When You Wear Sunscreen?
platforms.meta_description: Wearing SPF daily and the patches still darken? Visible light, screens and heat slip past a clear sunscreen — here is what dermatologists suggest instead.
platforms.body_html:
You put on sunscreen every morning, and the brown patches across your cheeks, forehead and upper lip still look deeper than they did last summer. That is one of the more discouraging things about melasma, and it is far from rare: Cleveland Clinic estimates that between 1.5% and 33% of the population develops it, that about 90% of those affected are women, and that 15% to 50% of pregnant women get it. The reason a single morning application often is not enough has less to do with discipline than with what an ordinary sunscreen actually blocks.

Why the Patches Darken in the First Place

Melasma shows up when melanocytes, the cells that give skin its color, become more active than usual and pour out extra melanin. The American Academy of Dermatology is candid that researchers still do not fully understand why this happens in some people, but the list of known triggers is consistent: sunlight, the rise in estrogen and progesterone during pregnancy, birth control pills, anti-seizure medications, drugs that make skin more sensitive to sunlight, thyroid disease, and tanning beds. Cleveland Clinic adds that 33% to 50% of people with melasma report a relative who has it too, which is part of why two people with identical sun habits can end up with very different faces.

Cleveland Clinic sums up the trigger side in one sentence: melanocytes make more melanin in response to light, heat, or ultraviolet radiation, or to hormonal stimulation. Read that list again and the usual advice, put on sunscreen in the morning, clearly covers only part of it.

The Triggers a Clear Sunscreen Leaves Open

The first gap is visible light. The AAD states plainly that visible light has been shown to worsen melasma, especially in people with darker skin tones, and its own recommendation is a tinted sunscreen containing iron oxide on top of an SPF of 30 or higher. A clear, untinted sunscreen filters ultraviolet, not the visible part of daylight, so it can leave that trigger entirely in play from the moment you step outside.

The second gap is screens. Cleveland Clinic lists LED light from televisions, laptops, phones and tablets among the possible causes of melasma, and it includes cutting down on screen time in its own self-care advice. This is a newer and much less settled line of evidence than sunlight, and a phone screen is dramatically dimmer than the sky, so it deserves curiosity rather than panic. Still, if your patches sit worst on the side of your face you hold a phone to, that is a pattern worth testing for a couple of weeks.

The third gap is heat. Cleveland Clinic groups infrared, meaning heat, with ultraviolet and visible light as forms of radiation that push melanocytes into producing more pigment. Long hot showers, saunas and leaning over a stove do not carry the weight sunlight does on any official trigger list, but heat belongs in the same family as light rather than in a separate harmless one. The AAD makes a related point about your bathroom shelf: if a skin care product burns or stings, it is irritating your skin, and that irritation may darken the very spots you are trying to fade.

What Changes Once You Close the Gaps

  • Reapply at least every two hours — the AAD's instruction is to apply sunscreen 15 minutes before going outside and to reapply at least every two hours, including on cloudy days and after swimming or sweating.
  • Make it tinted — broad-spectrum, water-resistant, SPF 30 or higher, with iron oxide alongside zinc oxide or titanium dioxide. The tint is the part that deals with visible light.
  • Put shade and a hat first — a wide-brimmed hat, ideally one with a UPF number printed on the label, plus sunglasses with UV protection.
  • Retire anything that stings — gentle, fragrance-free products only while the patches are active.
  • Skip tanning beds and sunlamps entirely — indoor tanning can worsen melasma and keep treatment from working at all.

Consistent sun protection is also what makes prescription treatment worth starting. Dermatologists commonly prescribe hydroquinone, which in the United States is no longer sold without a prescription, tretinoin paired with a mild corticosteroid, a triple combination cream, or gentler options such as azelaic acid, kojic acid or vitamin C applied to the skin; oral tranexamic acid is added for stubborn cases. Two things are worth knowing before you begin: results usually take 3 to 12 months, and the vitamin C on that list is a topical, not a supplement you swallow.

The Bottom Line

If you change one thing this week, change the sunscreen itself: a tinted, iron-oxide sunscreen at SPF 30 or higher, reapplied every two hours, closes the gap that a clear morning application leaves wide open. Melasma does no harm to your body, and it responds to consistency far more than to intensity. See a board-certified dermatologist if the patches are spreading, if they appeared soon after you started a new medication, or if you want to know which treatments suit your skin tone before spending money on them. This article is general information, not medical advice.
